skill.name: sharing-skills
skill.description: Guide contributors through sharing a reusable skill by creating a branch, committing changes, pushing to a fork, and opening a pull request.
skill.summary: Guides contributors through preparing and submitting reusable skills through a GitHub pull request.
skill.author: DYAI2025

security_audit.summary: The skill is primarily a documentation workflow for contributing skills through git and GitHub. Most hidden-path and URL alerts are benign setup references, but several examples contain real external commands that can push branches, create pull requests, or use shell interpolation. The packaged ZIP also remains a manual-review blind spot.

remediation.issue: Runnable git and gh examples can affect remote repositories.
remediation.suggestion: Add explicit confirmation steps before push, pull request creation, branch deletion, and any command that changes remote state.

remediation.issue: Shell interpolation examples use user-controlled skill names.
remediation.suggestion: Show a validation step for skill_name and quote paths consistently before using it in branch names, commit messages, or PR titles.
Prefer `git push --force-with-lease` and warn users to verify the branch name and remote before running it.
Manually inspect the archive contents or remove it from the package before publication.

semantic_findings.title: Force Push Troubleshooting Guidance
semantic_findings.description: The troubleshooting section recommends `git push -f origin your-branch` after rebasing. Force pushing can overwrite remote branch history if used on the wrong branch or without coordination.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The command is explicitly present in troubleshooting guidance. It is legitimate for a personal feature branch but risky enough to require safer wording and confirmation.

content.value_statement: Reusable skills often stay local because contributors lack a clear publishing workflow. This skill gives Claude, Codex, and Claude Code a structured process for preparing a branch, commit, push, and pull request.
actual_capabilities: Explains when a skill is suitable for upstream contribution.
Outlines a branch, commit, push, and pull request workflow.
Provides example git and GitHub CLI commands for contributors.
Includes troubleshooting notes for GitHub CLI and SSH setup.
Advises contributors to keep each skill in its own pull request.
limitations: Does not validate that a skill is safe or well tested by itself.
Requires an authenticated GitHub CLI and a configured fork.
Uses placeholder repository names that users must replace.
Includes commands that should be reviewed before execution.

use_cases.title: Publish a reusable local skill
use_cases.description: Turn a tested local skill into a clean branch and pull request for upstream review.

use_cases.title: Standardize skill contributions
use_cases.description: Give team members a consistent checklist for preparing one skill per pull request.

use_cases.title: Troubleshoot contribution setup
use_cases.description: Identify missing GitHub CLI authentication, SSH configuration, or merge conflict steps.

prompt_templates.title: Prepare my skill for sharing
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner contributor with one completed skill
prompt_templates.prompt: Use the sharing-skills process to help me prepare my local skill for an upstream pull request. Ask before running any git or gh command.

prompt_templates.title: Create a safe contribution checklist
prompt_templates.scenario: Contributor wants guidance before touching git state
prompt_templates.prompt: Review my skill contribution plan and produce a step-by-step checklist. Include validation, testing, branch creation, commit, push, and PR creation steps.

prompt_templates.title: Draft pull request content
prompt_templates.prompt: Help me draft the pull request title, summary, testing notes, and context for a new reusable skill contribution.

prompt_templates.title: Resolve contribution workflow issues
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced user hit authentication or merge conflicts
prompt_templates.prompt: Use the sharing-skills troubleshooting guidance to diagnose my failed contribution workflow. Recommend safe commands and ask before remote changes.

output_examples.input: I have a tested skill and want to share it upstream.
output: Confirms the skill is broad enough to share.
Checks that the local main branch is synced.
Suggests a feature branch name and commit message.
Drafts pull request text for review.

output_examples.input: My pull request has merge conflicts after upstream changed.
output: Explains how to fetch the latest upstream branch.
Warns before any force push and suggests safer remote update practices.

best_practices: Review every git and gh command before running it, especially commands that push to a remote.
Keep one skill per branch and one skill per pull request for easier review.
Test the skill with realistic prompts before creating the pull request.
anti_patterns: Do not batch unrelated skills into one pull request.
Do not share project-specific, sensitive, or unstable skills upstream.
Do not force push without verifying the target branch and remote.

faq.question: What does this skill help me do?
faq.answer: It guides you through sharing a reusable skill with an upstream repository through a GitHub pull request.

faq.question: Does it create the pull request automatically?
faq.answer: It provides commands and structure, but users should review and approve any command that changes git or GitHub state.

faq.question: What tools does it assume are available?
faq.answer: It assumes git and the GitHub CLI are installed, configured, and authenticated.

faq.question: Can I use it for private company skills?
faq.answer: Only if the skill is approved for sharing. The source guidance says to keep sensitive or organization-specific skills private.

faq.question: Why should each skill have its own pull request?
faq.answer: Separate pull requests make review, iteration, and merging easier for maintainers.

faq.question: Is the skill safe to install automatically?
faq.answer: It contains external command examples and an unscanned archive, so automated installers should treat it with caution.
